top_level_objectives: Represent physical quantities as vectors with magnitude and direction
Perform vector addition graphically using the tip-to-tail method
Decompose a vector into perpendicular components using right-triangle trigonometry
Apply vector decomposition to analyze the initial velocity of a projectile
Recognize that horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent
Predict and verify how launch angle and speed affect trajectory, range, and maximum height

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as arrows encoding both magnitude and direction, contrasting them with scalars, and let students build intuition by manipulating a simple vector in 3D space.
key_visuals: A floating arrow (vector) anchored at the origin of a 3D grid
Numeric readout of magnitude and direction angle next to the arrow
A comparison panel showing a scalar (plain number) versus the vector arrow
student_actions: Grab and drag the tip of the vector arrow to change its length and direction
Read off the resulting magnitude and angle values displayed
Answer a quick check-in question distinguishing a vector from a scalar example

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how two vectors combine into a resultant using the tip-to-tail method, building the foundation for combining velocity components later.
key_visuals: Two colored vectors (A and B) placed in the grid
An animated ghost copy of vector B sliding to the tip of vector A
The resultant vector R drawn from the tail of A to the tip of the relocated B
student_actions: Reposition vectors A and B by dragging their tips
Trigger the tip-to-tail animation to see the resultant form
Estimate the resultant's magnitude and direction before revealing the calculated values

scenes.brief_purpose: Show that any vector can be broken into horizontal and vertical components, reinforcing the trigonometric relationships needed for projectile analysis.
key_visuals: A single vector drawn at an angle above dashed x and y axes
Projected component vectors (x and y) shown as dashed lines dropping from the vector tip to each axis
A right triangle overlay labeling hypotenuse, adjacent, and opposite sides
student_actions: Rotate and resize the main vector using a handle
Toggle visibility of the x and y component vectors
Use the on-screen angle and magnitude to compute component values and check them against the displayed solution

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition from abstract vectors to a physical context by framing a projectile's initial velocity as a vector to be decomposed.
key_visuals: A small cannon or launcher model sitting on a horizontal platform
An initial velocity vector drawn from the launcher at an adjustable angle
Side-by-side numeric display of vx and vy as the angle slider changes
student_actions: Adjust a launch angle slider and observe the velocity vector rotate
Adjust a launch speed slider and observe the vector lengthen or shorten
Record the computed vx and vy for two or three different angle settings

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students fire the projectile and watch its parabolic path emerge, connecting the decomposed velocity components to real motion.
key_visuals: The launcher firing a ball that follows a parabolic arc
A trailing dotted path marking the trajectory already traveled
Live readouts of current horizontal position, vertical position, and elapsed time
student_actions: Press the launch button to fire the projectile at the chosen angle and speed
Pause the flight at a chosen instant to inspect the ball's current velocity vector
Observe how the vector's vertical arrow shrinks, vanishes, then grows downward while the horizontal arrow stays constant

scenes.scene_name: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Isolate and highlight the counterintuitive principle that horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes uniformly under gravity.
key_visuals: Two synchronized side panels: one showing only horizontal motion (constant-speed dot), one showing only vertical motion (accelerating up-down dot)
Overlaid graphs of vx versus time (flat line) and vy versus time (straight sloped line crossing zero at apex)
A combined view recombining both panels into the full parabolic trajectory
student_actions: Play the synchronized side-by-side animation and pause at the apex
Identify on the graphs where vertical velocity equals zero and relate it to the trajectory peak
Answer a prompt predicting what would happen to the trajectory if gravity were turned off

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students experiment freely with launch angle and speed to see how these choices affect range, maximum height, and flight time, tying together all prior concepts.
key_visuals: A distance-marked horizontal ground plane showing landing point
A height ruler showing the peak of the trajectory
A data table that logs angle, speed, range, and max height for each trial
student_actions: Set different combinations of launch angle and speed and fire multiple trials
Compare logged trials to find which angle maximizes range for a fixed speed
Formulate and record a short conclusion about the relationship between launch angle and range

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate the lab's key ideas by having students articulate the connection between vector operations and projectile motion in a final review.
key_visuals: A recap slideshow overlay cycling through key snapshots from earlier scenes
A final annotated diagram of a projectile trajectory with vx, vy, and resultant velocity vectors labeled at three points along the path
A short quiz panel floating above the launcher
student_actions: Label the velocity vectors at the launch point, apex, and landing point on the annotated diagram
Answer a short multiple-choice quiz covering vector addition, decomposition, and projectile independence
Reflect in a text box on how vector decomposition simplified analyzing the projectile's motion
